The Chinese sturgeon Acipenser sinensis is one of the largest freshwater fish species, with the ultimate total length of adults reaching up to 346 cm [Li = up to 346 cm]. This prodigious size is a hallmark of the species, which undertakes anadromous migrations within the Yangtze River system. Individuals begin their lives at a remarkably small size; upon hatching, the yolk-sac larva emerges with a wet weight of just 0.0156 grams [Wwb = 0.0156 grams], a direct consequence of the egg diameter which typically ranges from 2.7 to 3.4 mm. This tiny neonate must then navigate a perilous environment, and its growth trajectory is tightly linked to water temperature. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C], the early development and subsequent metabolic processes are optimized, though field studies suggest that natural thermal regimes can produce considerable variation in early growth rates.

Sexual maturation in Acipenser sinensis occurs at a total length of approximately 160 cm [Lp = approximately 160 cm], a benchmark that typically corresponds to an age of over a decade. At this size, the body mass of a pubertal individual is substantial, reaching an estimated 31,500 grams [Wwp = 31,500 grams]. This mass is achieved through a long juvenile phase characterized by sustained feeding and somatic growth. The length at puberty is particularly important for fisheries management, as it represents the minimum size at which individuals can contribute to the breeding population. The long delay before maturity is a classic feature of a K-selected life-history strategy, making the species especially vulnerable to overexploitation, as individuals are often captured before they have had the opportunity to spawn even once.

Reproductive output in this species is substantial, reflecting its large body size. Field observations indicate that a single sexually mature female can produce approximately 1,300,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,300,000 eggs per spawning event] and will spawn roughly once per year [F_R_i = spawn roughly once per year], with the overall maximum reproductive rate being best contextualized through these separate components. The enormous number of eggs released in a single spawning event is characteristic of many acipenserids. Crucially, these spawning events are heavily dependent on thermal conditions; the associated reproductive physiology has been studied at a water temperature of 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C], which appears to be near the optimal for gonadal recrudescence and gamete quality. Without the proper thermal cues, reproductive success can plummet.

The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown, aged Chinese sturgeon has been recorded at 362,600 grams [Wwi = 362,600 grams], a value that corresponds with the species' status as a giant among freshwater teleosts. This massive body size has significant ecological implications, dictating a high food intake and a position near the apex of the aquatic food web. The longevity that allows individuals to reach this size is notable. In captivity, with controlled feeding and the absence of predation, the maximum lifespan has been documented at 12,045 days [am = 12,045 days] under a stable thermal regime of 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C]. This extraordinary lifespan, equivalent to approximately 33 years, underscores the species' extremely slow life history, where every life stage from juvenile to adult is drawn out over many years.

The life-history of Acipenser sinensis is defined by its large size and slow pace. The total length at which a female first spawns, approximately 160 cm [Lp = approximately 160 cm], is a critical parameter for conservation. The enormous number of eggs released across a single clutch, around 1,300,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = around 1,300,000 eggs per spawning event], along with a spawning frequency of once per year [F_R_i = spawning frequency of once per year], means that an individual female has a very limited number of reproductive events in her lifetime. The long developmental period from a hatchling weighing 0.0156 grams [Wwb = 0.0156 grams] to a mature adult ensures that each individual has a high potential for growth, but also a long window of vulnerability. These synapomorphic traits of the species make any additional mortality from fishing a severe threat to population persistence.
